title: Ain Jalut, 1260
hook: the Mamluks of Egypt stop the Mongol advance in Palestine

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baghdad, the city of the caliphs, sacked, and a river the chronicles say ran dark with ink. Your line was: the river of ink. Which book did you look after? Day nine hundred sixty.

A letter arrives in Cairo. It comes from the Mongol camp, and the chronicles say it demands surrender, with threats to match. Baghdad has fallen. The cities of Syria have fallen or opened their gates. The sultan of Egypt, a soldier named Qutuz, has to answer. He could pay. He could wait behind the walls and hope. Instead, the chronicles say, he gathers his army and marches north, out of Egypt, to meet them. The two armies come face to face beside a spring in Palestine, a spring with a name out of an old story. Today's word is that place: Ain Jalut.
screen: `A LETTER DEMANDING SURRENDER.` → `QUTUZ MARCHES NORTH.` → `A SPRING WITH AN OLD NAME.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. 'Ayn is Arabic for a spring, and also for an eye. Jalut is the name the Qur'an gives to Goliath. So Ain Jalut is the spring of Goliath. And the Qur'an tells that story, in surah al-Baqarah. A king called Talut, often identified with Saul, leads an army out against Jalut. He tests his men at a river: whoever drinks from it isn't with me, he says, except one who scoops up a single handful. Most of them drink. Only a few hold back. And that small group, facing Jalut's army, says, in Pickthall's English: "How many a little company hath overcome a mighty host by Allah's leave! Allah is with the steadfast." They ask Allah for patience and for firm feet. Then, the Qur'an says, David killed Goliath. Now the battle. The Mamluk army met the Mongols at that spring, and the Mamluks won. The Mongol advance toward Egypt stopped there. Among Qutuz's commanders was a man named Baybars. And history doesn't end tidily: the chronicles say that on the way home Qutuz was killed by his own officers, and Baybars became sultan. So why does the name matter? Because for the people who told this story, the place seemed to speak. A spring named for Goliath, where an army that had seemed unstoppable was stopped. In this story, the people Allah is with are the steadfast, the ones who hold their ground. Holding your ground isn't the same as winning every fight. It means there's a line, and you stay on it.
screen: `'AYN — A SPRING, OR AN EYE.` · `TALUT, JALUT, AND A LITTLE COMPANY.` · `THE MONGOLS STOPPED AT THE SPRING.` · `ALLAH IS WITH THE STEADFAST.` · then, large: `THE SPRING OF GOLIATH.`

segments.voice: The practice: stand firm at one limit. Settle, and put both feet flat on the floor. Feel them there. Now think of one line in your life that keeps getting pushed: a habit you've said you'd stop, a request you keep saying yes to when you mean no, a boundary at work, with a phone, with a person. Name the line in a few words. Then picture the next time it gets tested, and see yourself staying on it, feet on the ground. If you pray, you can ask Allah for patience and firm feet, as the little company did. If you don't, simply hold the line in mind. The bell holds the time.
Ain Jalut. The spring of Goliath, in Palestine, where the Mamluks of Egypt stopped the Mongol advance. Today's word.
Your line: the spring of goliath. Today, when the line you named gets tested, feel your feet on the ground and stay on it once. Day nine hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Talut and Jalut in surah al-Baqarah, and its line that Allah is with the steadfast is often quoted in times of hardship.

fork.setup: you're Qutuz, sultan in Cairo. a letter from the Mongol camp demands surrender, and city after city has fallen. what do you do?
options: pay, and keep Egypt safe for now.
fork.reveal: the chronicles say he marched out of Egypt and met them at Ain Jalut, the spring of Goliath, and the Mamluks won.

original.note: Arabic: the spring of Goliath. 'ayn is a spring or an eye; Jalut is the Qur'an's name for Goliath.

trapdoor: what you thought: a battle with a hard name.
what it means: the spring of Goliath, where the Mamluks of Egypt stopped the Mongol advance.
what a scholar hears: Jalut from surah al-Baqarah, the little company that overcame a mighty host, and Qutuz killed on the way home, with Baybars made sultan.

sources.quoted: How many a little company hath overcome a mighty host by Allah's leave! Allah is with the steadfast.

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:246–251 (Talut, the river test, Jalut, David)
Mamluk-era chronicles, e.g. al-Maqrizi, al-Suluk (the letter, the march, the battle and Qutuz's death)

notes: No date, army sizes or casualty numbers given, under the claims rule; the year appears only in the index title.
Pickthall 2:249 quoted: 'How many a little company hath overcome a mighty host by Allah's leave! Allah is with the steadfast.' Confirm exact wording against the 1930 text.
'Most of them drink. Only a few hold back': the Qur'an says 'they drank thereof, all save a few of them' (2:249); confirm the paraphrase.
The petition for patience and firm feet (2:250) is described, not quoted.

The Mongol letter demanding surrender, Qutuz's march, and his killing on the way home with Baybars becoming sultan are paraphrased from the chronicles; accounts differ on details (including what happened to the envoys, left out). Confirm.
The script avoids calling Ain Jalut the Mongols' first defeat; it says only that their advance toward Egypt stopped there. Confirm.
'Ayn as both 'spring' and 'eye' is standard lexicon; confirm.
Editor: the river test now follows 2:249 more closely ('drinks from it', 'a single handful') instead of 'drinks his fill'.

Audit (y3 957-966): 'the word the Qur'an uses for the people Allah is with is the steadfast' overstated the text (the Qur'an also says Allah is with the God-fearing and the doers of good); now 'in this story, the people Allah is with are the steadfast'.
